exam: A 22‑year‑old with HIV presents with passive suicidal thoughts but no plan – what immediate actions are required? — Assess safety, involve family, arrange close observation, and start depression treatment; no need for involuntary admission yet.

A patient with bipolar disorder is currently depressed, drinking heavily, and says ‘I have a plan to overdose’. Which medication class should you avoid and why? — Avoid tricyclic antidepressants because they are highly toxic in overdose; choose an SSRI instead.

During a ward round you find a patient with recent TB treatment defaulting and expressing hopelessness. How does the infection influence suicide risk? — Chronic disease adds psychosocial stress and may cause neuro‑inflammation; treat TB promptly to reduce despair.

You have no access to a psychiatric inpatient unit. A patient has an imminent plan and access to pesticides. What is the safest next step? — Arrange emergency transfer to a facility with secure observation or, if impossible, keep the patient under constant bedside observation and remove the pesticides.

A patient with severe depression refuses food and fluids. What complication must you monitor for and how? — Risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance; monitor vitals, urine output, and electrolytes, and consider nasogastric feeding if refusal persists.

Explain how you would differentiate non‑suicidal self‑injury from a suicide attempt in a low‑resource setting. — Ask about intent to die; non‑suicidal self‑injury lacks desire to die and is often for relief of tension; document absence of plan and intent.

What psychosocial intervention is most feasible in a rural East African clinic for a patient with moderate suicide risk? — Brief problem‑solving therapy combined with family involvement and linkage to community health workers.

A patient on an SSRI reports worsening insomnia. What is the next appropriate step? — Evaluate for activation syndrome; consider adding low‑dose sleep hygiene measures or switching to a different antidepressant if insomnia persists.
ai.title: Suicide Risk Assessment and Management
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Suicide risk is the probability that a person will attempt or complete self‑harm. Assessment combines history, mental state, and risk factors, while management prioritises safety, treatment of underlying conditions, and follow‑up.

b: Suicidal ideation: thoughts of killing oneself
Suicidal plan: specific method or timing
Suicidal intent: desire to act on the plan
sections.p: Suicide risk refers to the likelihood of a patient attempting or completing self‑inflicted death. Diagnosis is clinical, based on reported thoughts, plans, intent, and behaviours.

b: Low: passive thoughts, no plan, no intent
Moderate: active thoughts, vague plan, no means
High: concrete plan, access to means, intent
Imminent: imminent act, prepared means, recent attempt
sections.p: Risk is stratified into low, moderate, high, and imminent based on the presence of intent, plan specificity, means availability, and past attempts.

b: Major depressive disorder – most frequent cause
Bipolar disorder – especially depressive pole
Alcohol use disorder – disinhibits impulse control
HIV, TB, malaria – chronic illness, stigma, pain
Recent loss, interpersonal conflict, financial stress
sections.p: Risk factors are grouped into psychiatric, medical, psychosocial, and environmental categories; the most common in low‑resource settings are psychiatric illness and chronic medical disease.

b: Verbal statements of hopelessness or “I’m a burden”
Sudden calm after a period of agitation (possible preparation)
Changes in sleep, appetite, or medication adherence
sections.p: Patients may verbalise hopelessness, express a plan, or show behavioural warning signs such as giving away possessions.
Testing focuses on identifying reversible medical contributors and confirming psychiatric diagnoses.

t.a: Full blood count, electrolytes, renal & liver panel
t.b: Detect metabolic derangements (e.g., hyponatraemia) that can worsen mood; treat if abnormal

t.a: HIV, hepatitis B/C serology, TB screening (GeneXpert if available)
t.b: Identify chronic infections that increase despair; start disease‑specific therapy
Detect substance use (alcohol, stimulants) that raises impulsivity; guide detox plan

t.a: Brief mental‑state exam (MMSE or MoCA if needed)
t.b: Assess cognition, psychosis, or delirium that may affect risk; treat underlying cause

b: Recent suicide attempt within 24 h
Access to lethal means (pesticides, firearms)
Severe psychotic depression or catatonia
Life‑threatening refusal of food/fluids
sections.p: Certain features demand urgent intervention to prevent death.

b: Immediate safety plan: remove means, constant observation, involve family
Psychotherapy: brief CBT or problem‑solving therapy, especially if resources limited
Pharmacology: start an SSRI for depression; consider low‑dose atypical antipsychotic if psychosis present; avoid tricyclics in overdose‑prone patients
Address alcohol misuse: brief counselling, referral for detox if possible
Treat comorbid infections (e.g., start anti‑TB therapy) to reduce hopelessness
sections.p: Safety first, then treat underlying psychiatric and medical problems; use evidence‑based psychosocial and pharmacologic strategies.

b: Re‑evaluate risk at each contact; document changes
Link to community mental‑health workers or peer support groups
Schedule follow‑up within 48 h after discharge from emergency
Educate family on warning signs and safe storage of medications
sections.p: Regular reassessment of risk, continuity of care, and community support reduce recurrence.

b: Non‑suicidal self‑injury – intent to harm without desire to die
Passive death wish – “I wish I could die” without plan or intent
sections.p: Distinguish suicidal ideation from non‑suicidal self‑injury and from passive death wishes.

b: Normal electrolytes despite severe dehydration – clinical picture matters
Negative urine toxicology when patient uses alcohol only – still high risk
sections.p: Normal labs do not rule out high suicide risk; some markers may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Presence of a concrete plan with means
Life‑threatening refusal of food or fluids
